\title{A stabilizer-rank backend for \texttt{clifft}:\\
       one compiler, two executors}
\author{Research note}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\texttt{clifft} simulates Clifford$+T$ circuits exactly, with a symbolic
Clifford frame and a dense $2^k$ active block whose size $k$ (the compiled
\emph{peak rank}) is the cost driver. We add a second executor: a low-rank
stabilizer (CH-form) backend whose cost driver is instead the circuit's live
magic --- $2^{0.228\,t}$ terms for $t$ live $T$-gates, at a tunable accuracy
$\delta$. Both cost exponents are known from a single \texttt{clifft}
compilation before anything runs, so execution becomes a per-program
dispatch: the dense engine where the compiled block is small (most circuits),
the backend where the block is large but magic is sparse. Measured against
\texttt{clifft}'s exact fast path on circuits that compile to genuinely large
blocks, the backend crosses over at $n\!\approx\!34$ (coarse accuracy) and
$n\!\approx\!48$ ($8\%$ error), and past $n\!\approx\!62$ --- where every
known exact method needs $16$\,GB--$1$\,TB --- it is the only method that
runs ($n{=}72$ in $267$\,s and $1.9$\,GB). Accuracy follows a clean measured
law, $\mathrm{TV}=(0.50\pm0.01)\,\delta$. The backend consumes
\texttt{clifft}'s optimized Heisenberg IR directly (which contains no
Clifford gates at all --- the compiler absorbs them), handles arbitrary
interleaved magic by $T$-gadgetization, adaptive feedforward circuits online,
and episode-structured circuits at a per-episode cost exponent
($m_{\rm blk}$ instead of $t$), all validated to machine precision against
\texttt{clifft} and an independent exact evaluator.
\end{abstract}

\section{The system in one view}\label{sec:arch}

\texttt{clifft}'s state is split into a \emph{symbolic Clifford frame}
(dormant axes evolve for free) and a \emph{dense active block}, a $2^k$
statevector expanded only for non-Clifford content. Two static facts scope
the design (\texttt{research/stabrank\_profiling}): $k$ is built from magic
--- plain Clifford superposition never inflates it --- and \texttt{clifft}'s
measurement-reordering passes shrink $k$ aggressively. When the block is
nevertheless large but \emph{magic-sparse}, its stabilizer rank is
$\ll 2^k$; the backend executes exactly that regime, at the cost of
exactness.

\paragraph{One compiler.} Every circuit goes through \texttt{clifft}'s
compiler regardless of which engine will execute it. Tracing produces the
Heisenberg IR: a remarkable object that contains \emph{no Clifford gates at
all} --- every Clifford is absorbed into the Pauli strings of the surviving
ops, so what remains is a sequence of $T$-rotations about arbitrary Paulis,
projective Pauli measurements, and classically-controlled Paulis
(feedforward). The optimization passes then merge magic ($T\!\cdot\!T\to S$
and similar), leaving the \emph{live} $T$-count $t_{\rm live}$, and reorder
measurements as early as they commute --- which is what keeps the compiled
peak rank $k$ small, usually far smaller than the qubit count.

\paragraph{Two executors, dispatched at compile time.} The compiled artifact
carries every quantity the routing decision needs:

The dispatcher (\texttt{dispatch.py}) prices four strategies from one
compilation and routes each program to the cheapest feasible one:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
strategy & cost ($\log_2$ dominant term) & guarantee & inputs \\
\midrule
dense engine & $k$ & exact & $k=\mathrm{peak\_rank}$ \\
backend, global & $0.228\,t_{\rm live} + 2\log_2\!\frac1\delta$ & $\delta$-approx.\ & $t_{\rm live}$ (HIR) \\
backend, episodic-exact & $m_{\rm blk}$ & exact & $m_{\rm blk}$, $R$ (profiler) \\
backend, episodic-approx.\ & $0.228\,m_{\rm blk} + 2\log_2\!\frac{R}{\delta}$ & $\delta$-approx.$^\dagger$ & $m_{\rm blk}$, $R$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
{\small $m_{\rm blk}$ = peak $T$-count within a single \emph{episode} (one
grow-and-fully-collapse cycle of the active block); $R$ = episode count.
$^\dagger$measured caveat for full-record targets, \S\ref{sec:episodic}.}

Representative routings (\texttt{dispatch.py} demo, $\delta{=}0.15$): dense
IQP at $n{=}40$ ($k{=}20$, $t{=}40$) $\to$ backend-global; random
Clifford$+T$ and hidden shift (which compile to $k\le10$) $\to$ dense; a
feedforward conveyor with $12$ rounds of $128$ $T$'s ($k{=}49$: dense
infeasible; $0.228\cdot1536\approx350$: global absurd) $\to$
backend-episodic, the only strategy that runs.

\paragraph{What comes from where.} The backend borrows \texttt{clifft}'s two
architectural ideas --- the global symbolic Clifford frame and
measurement-driven collapse of the non-Clifford core --- and re-instantiates
them over a different core: BGH's low-rank CH-form sum~\cite{bravyi2019}
instead of a dense $2^k$ array. The simulation mathematics (CH-form,
minimal-extent decomposition, sparsification, norm estimation, gadgetization)
is BGH/Bravyi--Gosset throughout; none of \texttt{clifft}'s runtime is used.
\texttt{clifft} serves as compiler front-end (the backend consumes its
optimized HIR directly, \S\ref{sec:hir}), as validation oracle (every
component is checked against it to machine precision), and as the exact
opponent in every benchmark.

\paragraph{Design commitments.} (i) The backend is an explicit opt-in
($\delta$), never a silent substitute: when exactness is demanded past the
memory wall, the honest answer is ``infeasible'' --- \texttt{clifft}'s
exactness contract is untouched. (ii) Both executors consume the same
compiled stream, so every compiler improvement (magic merging, measurement
reordering, fusion) lowers both engines' costs. (iii) Baseline discipline:
all comparisons below run against \texttt{clifft}'s true fast path ---
\texttt{record\_probabilities} on the \emph{measured} program --- and are
cross-checked by an independent exact evaluator; comparing against the
unitary path ($\mathrm{peak\_rank}=n$) would overstate the backend by orders
of magnitude and is never done here.

In one sentence: \texttt{clifft}'s architecture is the blueprint, BGH's
mathematics is the material, and \texttt{clifft} itself is the compiler
front-end that decides --- per program, before execution --- which executor
runs.

\section{Background and related work}
\paragraph{CH-form and low-rank decompositions.}
A stabilizer state is stored as $\ket{\phi}=\omega\,U_C U_H \ket{s}$
(Bravyi--Browne--Calpin--Campbell--Gosset--Howard~\cite{bravyi2019}): $O(n^2)$
bits per term, $O(n)$ Clifford gates, $O(n^2)$ Hadamard and single-amplitude
queries. A magic state is a sum $\ket\psi=\sum_a c_a\ket{\phi_a}$ of $\chi$
terms; Cliffords preserve $\chi$, each $T$ doubles it, measurement can
collapse it.

\paragraph{Related work.}
``Cliffords paid once, exponential cost only on the magic'' is the
architecture of Bravyi--Gosset~\cite{bravyi2016}; Qassim, Wallman and
Gosset~\cite{qassim2019} recompile circuits into non-Clifford rotations times
a single global Clifford precisely to speed up CH-form simulators;
Garc\'ia--Markov~\cite{garcia2015} shared a stabilizer frame across
superposition terms; Pauli-based computation~\cite{peres2023} absorbs all
Cliffords into adaptive Pauli measurements on $t$ magic qubits. The closest
single work is Pashayan et al.~\cite{pashayan2022}: gadgetize the $T$'s, then
\emph{statically} compress the global Clifford and the outcome projector
before running a stabilizer-rank estimator. Stabilizer tensor networks with
magic injection~\cite{nakhl2025} pair a Clifford frame with an MPS residual;
\texttt{quizx}~\cite{kissinger2022} reaches ``decompose only the magic'' via
ZX rewriting. What this system adds is the \emph{online} form of the
composition --- a compiler-maintained global frame over a CH-form term sum,
with dynamic measurement-driven collapse and mid-circuit/adaptive measurement
--- plus the engineering observation (verified in qiskit-aer's source) that
the flagship open-source CH-form simulator, \texttt{extended\_stabilizer},
applies every Clifford per-term at $O(\chi)$ cost, with no frame. The
composition's advantage is a constant/poly factor, never an exponent, and we
claim nothing more for it.

\section{Theory}\label{sec:theory}

\subsection{Minimal-extent magic decomposition (the $0.228$ exponent)}
$T = \alpha I + \beta S$ with
$\alpha=\tfrac12+i\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}{2}$, $\beta=\bar\alpha$, both terms
Clifford, $|\alpha|+|\beta| = 2^{0.114}$, so the stabilizer extent per $T$ is
$2^{0.228}$ --- optimal within the extent framework, since extent is
multiplicative for tensor products of single-qubit states~\cite{bravyi2019}.
Branching in the computational basis instead costs extent $2^t$, which
sparsification cannot repair; this basis choice is the crux.

\subsection{Single-shot sampling, and gadgetization for general circuits}
\label{sec:gadget-theory}
Importance-sampling $k$ terms from $p_a=|c_a|/\lVert c\rVert_1$ gives an
unbiased $\ket\omega$ with
$\mathbb{E}\lVert\ket\psi-\ket\omega\rVert^2=(\lVert c\rVert_1^2-\lVert\psi\rVert^2)/k$;
$k\sim 2^{0.228t}/\delta^2$ bounds the 2-norm error by $\delta$. For
\emph{product} magic (one $T$-layer, as in IQP) the branch strings factorize
and are sampled directly --- unbiased, no $2^t$ built, no factor-$t$ variance
accumulation (streaming mid-circuit sparsification pays that factor; it is
implemented but not the benchmarked path).

Arbitrary circuits with interleaved magic reduce to this case by
\textbf{$T$-gadgetization}: teleport each in-line $T$ onto its own ancilla
and force the gadget outcome to $0$. Since the gadget's
classically-controlled correction makes all outcome branches equivalent, the
$0$-branch alone carries the answer --- each forced-$0$ gadget contributes
exactly $T/\sqrt2$, so
$P(x) = 2^{t}\,|\bra{x,0^t} C_{\rm gadget} (\ket{0^n}\!\otimes\!\ket{T}^{\otimes t})|^2$
with $C_{\rm gadget}$ entirely Clifford. All magic is again one product
layer: the single-shot sampler applies with no streaming penalty, and the
normalization stays analytic (\S\ref{sec:norm-theory}).

\subsection{Episodic execution}\label{sec:episodic-theory}
Long computations \emph{recycle} magic: the active core grows and fully
collapses again (an \emph{episode}), so the per-episode magic $m_{\rm blk}$
stays bounded while $t_{\rm live}$ grows with runtime. The backend exploits
this by running one episode at a time. The sound schedule, each element
load-bearing (measured in \S\ref{sec:episodic}):
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Sparsify at $T$-time only.} The resample is well-conditioned
only when $\lVert c\rVert_1$ is extent-controlled, which holds for the
$T$-branching of a freshly collapsed base. It is \emph{never} applied after a
projection: forced measurements inflate
$\lVert c\rVert_1/\lVert\psi\rVert$ (cancellation) and make the resample
ill-conditioned.
\item \textbf{Collapse exactly at boundaries.} When an episode has fully
collapsed the state is rank 1; the collapse is a deterministic
amplitude-ratio sum at an analytic tableau support point ($x^*=Gs$ over
$\mathbb{F}_2$, using $F^{-1}=G^\top$), detected by a two-probe parallelism
test (\texttt{collapse\_if\_parallel}) --- $O(\chi n^2)$, no $2^n$ scan.
\item \textbf{Debias with two independent runs.} The naive estimator
$\lVert\Pi\omega\rVert^2$ is biased upward by the sparsification variance;
the cross estimator $\langle\Pi\omega|\Pi\omega'\rangle$ of two independent
runs is unbiased, and at rank-1 endings reduces to two amplitudes at one
support point.
\item \textbf{Keep episodes contiguous.} Episodic mode uses the compiler's
magic-merging pass only (\texttt{PeepholeFusionPass}); the
measurement-hoisting pass would interleave episodes and defeat the boundary
collapse.
\end{itemize}
At budget $2^{m_{\rm blk}}$ (episodic-exact) no resample ever fires and the
run is exact at cost exponent $m_{\rm blk}$, deterministically. Below that
budget the run is unbiased but approximate, with errors compounding over the
$R$ boundaries --- the compounding law is measured in \S\ref{sec:episodic}.

\subsection{Normalization}\label{sec:norm-theory}
$P(x)=|\bra x\psi\rangle|^2/\lVert\psi\rVert^2$ needs $\lVert\psi\rVert^2$
without materializing $2^n$. Three regimes, in order of preference:
\emph{analytic} --- for unitary product magic (including everything
gadgetized) $\lVert\psi\rVert=1$ and
$\mathbb{E}\lVert\omega\rVert^2 = 1+(\lVert c\rVert_1^2-1)/k$ exactly, so no
estimation enters; \emph{rank-1} --- at fully-collapsed endings the norm is
an $O(\chi n^2)$ amplitude-ratio sum; \emph{estimated} --- the BGH estimator
(Lemmas 2--4, $O(n^3)$ exponential sum) otherwise. The estimator's
per-sample relative spread is $\approx\!1.2$, so $L$ samples cost
$\approx\!1.2/\sqrt L$ relative error on every reported probability; keeping
that subdominant for generic circuits scales as
$\chi L \sim 2^{0.228t}/\delta^4$ --- the pipeline's one real accuracy-cost
bottleneck, stated as such. Quoted accuracies always include the
normalization term.

\subsection{Error guarantee, stated precisely}\label{sec:guarantee}
Sparsification bounds the \emph{2-norm} error
$\lVert\psi-\omega\rVert\le\delta$. For a single target that yields an
\emph{additive} amplitude error of typical size $\delta\,2^{-n/2}$ --- i.e.\ a
$\sim\!\delta$ \emph{relative} error on \emph{typical} (anticoncentrated)
probabilities $P(x)\sim2^{-n}$, which is what the measured
$\mathrm{TV}\approx0.5\,\delta$ law reflects. It is \textbf{not} a per-$x$
relative-error guarantee: individual small probabilities can be off by more.
Guaranteed relative error costs the exact-rank methods
($2^{0.396t}$~\cite{qassim2021}); multiplicative approximation remains
GapP-hard for $T$-type IQP~\cite{bremner2016}, so there is no poly-time
escape.

\subsection{The online frame, for adaptive circuits}\label{sec:frame-theory}
For circuits the compiler can see through, the Heisenberg IR already
delivers ``free Cliffords'' statically. For \emph{dynamic} circuits ---
mid-circuit measurement with data-dependent control the compiler cannot
resolve --- the backend maintains the frame online:
$\ket{\mathrm{state}}=F(\sum_a\ket{\phi_a})$ with $F$ a global Clifford
updated in $O(n)$ per gate; magic and measurement act on the terms conjugated
through $F$ at the optimal $\{I,S\}$ extent. The frame does not eliminate
per-term work; it \emph{moves} it from Cliffords onto magic and measurement
(conjugated operators $P'=F^{-1}PF$ have weight $\sim w$, costing $O(w)$
per-term applications per $T$ and per measurement). That is why the frame
pays off only on Clifford-dominated adaptive circuits --- the measured phase
boundary of \S\ref{sec:adaptive}.

\section{Implementation and validation}\label{sec:impl}
A Python engine (\texttt{research/chform\_backend}) is the reference
implementation --- including the HIR bridge, gadgetization, episodic
execution, the online frame, and the dispatcher --- and a standalone
bit-packed C\texttt{++}20 port (\texttt{research/chform\_cpp}) is the
performance implementation for the build-and-query pipeline (single-shot
magic $+$ Clifford stream $+$ amplitude/norm queries; amplitudes are
word-based, and the multi-word $n>64$ paths are covered by tests). Ground
truth everywhere is \texttt{clifft}'s exact \texttt{record\_probabilities},
independently cross-validated by a meet-in-the-middle evaluator
(\texttt{mitm\_iqp.cpp}): exact $P(x)$ for any $T{+}CZ$ IQP circuit in
$O(n2^{n/2})$ time and $2^{n/2}$ memory --- ground truth to $n\!\approx\!62$
on a $36$\,GB machine, and incidentally the fastest exact method on that
family.

\subsection{Consuming the compiler's output}\label{sec:hir}
The backend reads \texttt{clifft}'s optimized HIR directly
(\texttt{hir\_bridge.py}, via the exposed
\texttt{parse}$\to$\texttt{trace}$\to$\texttt{HirPassManager} pipeline). The
IR's op types map one-to-one onto the engine's explicit-Pauli primitives:
$T$-rotations about arbitrary Paulis (\texttt{rz\_about\_pauli}), projective
Pauli measurements (\texttt{measure\_pauli\_forced\_fast}), and conditional
Paulis (feedforward, deterministic under a forced record). Consequences,
measured: the backend performs \emph{zero} Clifford gate applications on any
compiled circuit; $\chi$ tracks $2^{t_{\rm live}}$ and often less (the
compiler's hoisted measurements collapse terms mid-run --- $\chi_{\rm peak}=8$
where $2^{t_{\rm live}}=64$ on one family); and $t_{\rm live}$ is roughly
half of the raw $T$-count on random circuits ($32/40/48 \to 18/28/28$), which
is why the dispatch rule uses it. For compile-known circuits the compiler
thus supersedes the online frame of \S\ref{sec:frame-theory}, which remains
the mechanism for dynamic circuits. The C\texttt{++} scale arm currently
consumes plain gate streams; feeding it HIR needs a simultaneous reduction of
the terminal Pauli measurements (a symplectic elimination) --- future work,
so its benchmark numbers below are conservative for the backend.

\section{Benchmarks}\label{sec:bench}
Contestants run single-threaded on an Apple M-series workstation ($36$\,GB;
\texttt{clifft} on its scalar/NEON path); the MitM ground truth uses all
cores but competes with no one. Scripts and raw JSON are committed. Measured
component facts: the $L_1$ growth per $T$ is exactly $2^{0.114}$;
sparsification error tracks the BGH bound to $\sim\!1\%$; the single-shot
estimator is unbiased. Figure~\ref{fig:families} sketches the four circuit
families that carry the measurements.

\subsection{The crossover}\label{sec:overlap}
Head-to-head on circuits that compile to \emph{genuinely large} blocks:
dense random IQP (CZ on each pair w.p.\ $\tfrac12$; the measured program
compiles to $\mathrm{peak\_rank}=n/2$, so the exact baseline scales as
$2^{n/2}$ --- as does MitM; everything exact costs $2^{n/2}$ on this
family). $96$ uniform targets, ground truth by MitM cross-checked against
\texttt{record\_probabilities}; backend at budget $k=2^{0.228n}/\delta^2$,
analytic normalization, timing includes build $+$ normalization $+$ all
amplitude evaluations; the error metric charges the full pipeline,
$\mathrm{TV}=\tfrac12\sum_x|\hat P(x)-P(x)|/\sum_x P(x)$. Means over 3
realizations ($n\le48$; 1 above):

\begin{table}[h]\centering
\caption{Exact fast path vs approximate backend (seconds for 96 $P(x)$).}
\label{tab:overlap}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrrrr}
\toprule
$n$ & $k_{\mathrm{meas}}$ & \texttt{clifft} exact & ours $\delta{=}0.4$ & TV & ours $\delta{=}0.15$ & TV \\
\midrule
24 & 12 & \textbf{0.003} & 0.09 & 0.070 & 0.08 & 0.070 \\
32 & 16 & \textbf{0.06} & 0.15 & 0.140 & 0.50 & 0.073 \\
36 & 18 & 0.27 & \textbf{0.18} & 0.192 & 1.22 & 0.081 \\
40 & 20 & 0.77 & \textbf{0.41} & 0.175 & 2.94 & 0.079 \\
44 & 22 & 4.1 & \textbf{1.0} & 0.194 & 7.4 & 0.076 \\
48 & 24 & 17.3 & \textbf{2.4} & 0.197 & \textbf{16.9} & 0.082 \\
52 & 26 & 92.9 & \textbf{5.5} & 0.186 & \textbf{39.4} & 0.074 \\
56 & 28 & 398 & \textbf{12.1} & 0.165 & \textbf{86.2} & 0.078 \\
60 & 30 & $\ge$16\,GB, skipped & \textbf{27.7} & 0.185 & \textbf{196} & 0.086 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The crossover sits at $n\!\approx\!34$ for $\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.17$ and
$n\!\approx\!48$ for $\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.08$; \texttt{clifft}'s exact
path grows as $2^{n/2}$ on the nose ($\times4.6$ per $+4$ qubits) and exits
at $n\!\approx\!58$--$62$ on memory, while the backend grows as $2^{0.228n}$
($\times1.9$ per $+4$). The axis is the \emph{compiled peak rank}, not the
qubit count: on families whose measured programs compile small
(nearest-neighbour-CZ chains: $\mathrm{peak\_rank}=1$; generic random
circuits: $\le6$), \texttt{clifft} answers in microseconds and the backend
has no role --- the dispatch rule of \S\ref{sec:arch} encodes exactly this.

\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{chform_cpp/honest_bench.png}
\caption{\emph{Left:} seconds for 96 Born probabilities on measured dense
IQP: \texttt{clifft}'s exact forced-replay path vs the CH-form backend at two
accuracy settings; the dotted guide is $2^{n/2}$. \emph{Right:} the accuracy
dial at $n{=}44$: full-pipeline TV against exact $P(x)$ vs the target
$\delta$, with the $\mathrm{TV}=0.50\,\delta$ line.}
\label{fig:honest}
\end{figure}

\subsection{The accuracy dial}\label{sec:precision}
At $n{=}44$, $256$ targets, $4$ realizations, analytic normalization
(Fig.~\ref{fig:honest}, right): $\mathrm{TV}=0.144(4),\,0.101(3),\,0.0500(6),
\,0.0251(3)$ at $\delta=0.30,0.20,0.10,0.05$ --- i.e.\
$\mathrm{TV}=(0.50\pm0.01)\,\delta$, with runtime
$\propto k\propto1/\delta^2$ ($2.0\to73.9$\,s). The law holds for the full
pipeline where normalization is analytic; with an $L{=}30$ estimated norm the
same budgets degrade by up to $\sim\!2\times$ on unlucky draws ($0.07$--$0.32$
observed vs $0.07$--$0.21$ analytic), exactly the
$1.2/\sqrt{30}\approx22\%$ multiplicative noise of \S\ref{sec:norm-theory}
--- the normalization term belongs in any quoted accuracy.

\subsection{The frontier}\label{sec:frontier}
Dense IQP, $\delta{=}0.4$, single-shot build $+$ one amplitude
(\texttt{bench\_iqp.cpp}); the exact column is what any known exact method
pays on this family.

\begin{table}[h]\centering
\caption{Past-exact frontier (dense IQP, $\delta{=}0.4$).}\label{tab:frontier}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrr}
\toprule
$n$ & $\chi$ & build & CH-form mem & exact $2^{n/2}$ mem \\
\midrule
40 & 3\,477   & 0.4\,s & 3.6\,MB  & 16\,MB (feasible) \\
50 & 16\,889  & 3.0\,s & 22\,MB   & 512\,MB (feasible) \\
60 & 82\,029  & 25\,s  & 128\,MB  & 16\,GB (marginal) \\
66 & 211\,728 & 82\,s  & 683\,MB  & 137\,GB (infeasible) \\
72 & 546\,497 & 267\,s & 1.9\,GB  & 1.1\,TB (infeasible) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Exact ground truth exists to $n\!\approx\!62$ (MitM), where the measured TV
still follows the dial ($0.086$ at $n{=}60$, $\delta{=}0.15$). At
$n{=}66$--$72$ no exact check exists (that is the point); accuracy there
rests on the $\delta$-law holding at every checkable size, the analytic
normalization being exact for this family, and the multi-word code paths
being tested (Table~\ref{tab:valid}) --- an extrapolation, stated as such.

\subsection{Generality: gadgetized circuits}\label{sec:gadget}
The gadgetized route (\S\ref{sec:gadget-theory}) handles arbitrary
interleaved magic at the product-magic price
(\texttt{gadgetize.py}; C\texttt{++} arm \texttt{bench\_gadget.cpp}); the
norm-estimation bottleneck of \S\ref{sec:norm-theory} never enters, since
normalization stays analytic. At scale, the hidden-shift family
(bent-function construction, CCZ oracles, $14$ $T$'s per CCZ) provides
\emph{built-in exact ground truth}: the output is the shift $s$
deterministically, so $P(s)=1$ at any size. Measured at $\delta=0.3$:
$n{=}16/24/32/40$ ($t=28$--$56$, up to $96$ total qubits) give
$\hat P(s) = 0.99/0.94/0.90/0.92$ in $0.1$--$8$\,s, with
$\hat P(x\!\neq\!s)=0$. On random interleaved Clifford$+T$ vs \texttt{clifft}
exact (targets sampled from the output distribution --- the likelihood
use-case): TV $0.04$--$0.09$ at $\delta=0.15$. These families validate
generality rather than exhibit a win regime: \texttt{clifft} compiles both to
$\mathrm{peak\_rank}\le10$ and answers exactly in microseconds --- which is
precisely the dispatch rule at work.

\subsection{Adaptive workloads and the phase boundary}\label{sec:adaptive}
For dynamic circuits the online frame (\S\ref{sec:frame-theory}) is measured
against a plain per-term engine (the architecture of Aer's
\texttt{extended\_stabilizer}, verified in its source) on identical
trajectories --- same circuits, same forced outcomes, same term store and
measurement code; only who pays for Cliffords differs. All engine variants
agree to $3\times10^{-16}$. On a synthetic sweep (a width-$w$ register,
rounds of feedforward $+$ $T^\pm$ layer $+$ $D$ global Clifford scrambling
layers applied \emph{while} $\chi=2^w$): frame time is flat in $D$
($6.9$--$7.9$\,s from $D{=}4$ to $96$ at $w{=}8$) while per-term time grows
linearly ($3.1\to65.9$\,s); the crossover sits at $D^*\!\approx\!1.2w$, with
$8.4\times$ at $D{=}96$ and growing (Fig.~\ref{fig:extadapt}, right). Below
the boundary the frame costs up to $\sim\!2\times$ --- the conjugation price
of \S\ref{sec:frame-theory}: at $w{=}12$, $D{=}4$ the plain engine spends
$68$\,s on per-term Cliffords where the frame spends $3$\,ms, yet the frame
loses overall because the moved work lands on magic and measurement.

\paragraph{Natural protocols land on the winning side.} Two recognizable
families locate real protocols relative to the boundary
(\texttt{bench\_natural.py}; identical-trajectory replay as above):
\emph{cultivation-style patches} --- a data register accumulates injected
$T$'s while every round runs syndrome extraction (ancilla CX fans,
measurements, classically-controlled corrections, ancilla reuse) plus $L$
layers of code-preserving logical Clifford traffic --- and
\emph{teleported-$T$ injection}, the textbook adaptive magic gadget.
Measured (8 data qubits, 7 checks, up to 10 injected $T$'s, $\chi$ up to
$\sim\!10^3$):

\begin{table}[h]\centering
\caption{Natural adaptive workloads: plain (per-term Cliffords) vs frame,
identical trajectories.}\label{tab:natural}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
workload & Cliffords/round & frame speedup \\
\midrule
bare syndrome extraction ($L{=}0$) & $\sim$14 & $0.8$--$1.0\times$ (at the boundary) \\
$+$ 1 logical-traffic layer & $\sim$32 & $3.7$--$6.7\times$ \\
$+$ 4 layers & $\sim$68 & $7$--$16\times$ \\
teleported-$T$ gadget & $\sim$4/gadget & $1.7$--$2.8\times$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Bare syndrome extraction sits exactly at the boundary; any logical Clifford
traffic pushes the composition into clear wins --- the plain engine's
per-term Clifford work is the entire gap ($11.8$\,s of a $12.0$\,s round set
vs the frame's $7$\,ms). One physical constraint the experiment surfaced: the
logical traffic must be \emph{code-preserving} (diagonal $+$ CNOT-type; no
bare $H$ on data), else the syndrome round measures the accumulated magic
away --- true of the toy and of the real protocols it models. Context that
sharpens the niche: qiskit-aer \texttt{extended\_stabilizer} \emph{rejects}
dynamic circuits outright (\texttt{mark}/\texttt{jump} unsupported), so
online adaptive CH-form simulation is territory the flagship open-source
implementation does not serve at all.

\subsection{Episodic execution, measured}\label{sec:episodic}
The episodic strategy (\S\ref{sec:episodic-theory}) is measured on
feedforward conveyors against \texttt{clifft}'s exact record probabilities
(\texttt{bench\_episodic.py}).

\begin{table}[h]\centering
\caption{Episodic accuracy vs budget (conveyor, 6 episodes of 8 $T$'s; exact
per-episode rank $2^8{=}256$; 24 repetitions; exact
$P(\mathrm{record})=1.15\times10^{-14}$).}\label{tab:episodic}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrr}
\toprule
budget $k$ & naive rel-rms & naive bias & cross rel-rms & cross bias \\
\midrule
32  & 2.86 & $+1.70$ & 1.14 & $-0.004$ \\
64  & 1.38 & $+0.71$ & 0.51 & $-0.199$ \\
128 & 0.57 & $+0.10$ & 0.41 & $+0.047$ \\
256 & 0.40 & $+0.07$ & 0.25 & $-0.024$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The budget sweep (Table~\ref{tab:episodic}) shows the cross estimator doing
its job: at $k{=}32$ the naive estimator carries a $+1.70$ bias where the
cross estimator is unbiased to $-0.004$. Headline results.
\emph{Episodic-exact}: at budget $2^{m_{\rm blk}}$ the run is exact
($\chi_{\rm peak}=2^{m_{\rm blk}}$, $P$ matching \texttt{clifft} to machine
precision) --- cost exponent $m_{\rm blk}$ instead of $t_{\rm live}$,
deterministically. \emph{Scale}: a $72$-qubit conveyor ($t_{\rm live}=72$;
whole-circuit $\chi$ would be $2^{72}$) runs end to end with no $2^n$ object
at $\chi\le400$, returning the record probability within $41\%$ relative at
$10\times$ per-episode compression (mean of four cross estimates, $66$\,s).
\emph{The measured limit}: for full-record probabilities the error turns on
sharply below the exact budget and compounds steeply with the episode count
(rel-rms $16$ at $R{=}8$, $110$ at $R{=}16$ even at $2\times$ compression) ---
the dispatcher's $R^2$ cost model is optimistic there; episodic-exact or mild
compression is the prescription for record targets, and the dispatcher prices
both.

\paragraph{Is a $10^{-22}$ probability meaningful?} Yes --- it is
\emph{typical}, not pathological: a $72$-bit record has probability
$\sim2^{-72}\approx2\times10^{-22}$ if outcomes were uniform, so this is the
natural size of \emph{any} full-record probability at this width. Relative
accuracy is therefore the right metric, and constant-factor accuracy of such
quantities is exactly what likelihood workflows consume (cross-entropy
benchmarking scores, per-record likelihood ratios, decoder likelihoods; a
$41\%$ relative error is $0.34$ nats of log-likelihood, averaging out over
records since the estimator is unbiased). No sampling method can access these
quantities at all ($\sim10^{22}$ shots for one expected hit --- the measured
$0/96$ aer result of \S\ref{sec:external} is the same phenomenon at $n{=}24$).
Conversely, applications needing only marginals or expectation values face
polynomially-sized targets, where the record-probability breakdown regime is
not the binding constraint.

\subsection{External tools}\label{sec:external}
On the same dense-IQP instances and targets as \S\ref{sec:overlap}
(\texttt{bench\_external.py}, everything validated against MitM):
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{QuiZX}~\cite{kissinger2022} (v0.3.0) computes each probability
exactly, one ZX-simplify$+$decompose run per target; its per-amplitude cost
grows at the exact-rank rate $2^{0.396n}$ (measured term counts
$301\to1.9\times10^6$ over $n{=}24\to56$: ZX simplification does not compress
dense $T{+}CZ$ IQP). For 96 targets: $0.5/251/2188$\,s at $n{=}24/48/56$ ---
vs this backend's $0.3/17/89$\,s at $\mathrm{TV}\approx0.08$, and vs MitM's
$0.4/4.7/84.5$\,s \emph{exactly}. Two qualifiers: QuiZX answers a harder
(exact) question, and on pure $T{+}CZ$ IQP the structure-specific MitM ties
the approximate backend through $n\!\approx\!56$ --- the backend's edge over
\emph{all} exact methods opens past the $2^{n/2}$ wall or off the IQP
structure.
\item \textbf{Quokka\#}~\cite{mei2024} (with its GPMC model counter, built
locally): exact per-amplitude, $3.1$\,s at $n{=}24$ (correct to
$5\times10^{-15}$) but timeout ($>300$\,s/amplitude) already at $n{=}32$ ---
the dense CZ graph defeats the CNF encoding far below the tool's published
sparse-circuit range. External exact ranking on this family: QuiZX $\gg$
Quokka\#, with MitM fastest of all three.
\item \textbf{qiskit-aer \texttt{extended\_stabilizer}}
(\texttt{bench\_aer.py}; aer $0.17.2$, settings inline): a sampling-only
tool. On sampling, \texttt{clifft} sustains $1.8$--$4.4\times10^6$ exact
shots/s ($\mathrm{peak\_rank}=1$ families) vs aer's approximate
$2721\to44$ shots/s over $n=10\to28$ --- ratios $1630\times$ to
$40{,}000\times$. On strong simulation it cannot enter: estimating $96$
targets with true $P\sim5.6\times10^{-8}$ at $n{=}24$, $30{,}000$ shots
($455$\,s) hit $0/96$; \texttt{clifft} answers exactly in $3.5$\,ms. The
three-way split: \texttt{clifft} owns exact work while $2^{n/2}$ fits; this
backend owns approximate $P(x)$ beyond; \texttt{extended\_stabilizer}
(sampling-only, maintenance-frozen upstream) is dominated on both tasks.
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{chform_cpp/external_adaptive.png}
\caption{\emph{Left:} external head-to-head on shared dense-IQP instances:
QuiZX (exact, per-target) vs the MitM evaluator (exact) vs this backend
(approximate, $\mathrm{TV}\approx0.08$), seconds for 96 probabilities.
\emph{Right:} the adaptive-workload phase boundary at $w{=}8$: plain
(per-term Cliffords) grows linearly in Clifford depth $D$; the frame
composition is flat; crossover at $D^*\!\approx\!1.2w$.}
\label{fig:extadapt}
\end{figure}

\section{Limitations}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Approximate}, with the guarantee of \S\ref{sec:guarantee}
(additive/typical, not per-$x$ relative); the dense engine remains the tool
wherever exactness is required and feasible.
\item \textbf{The exact competition is $2^{n/2}$, not $2^n$}, on the
benchmark family; the backend's genuinely-unique regime starts near
$n\!\approx\!62$, and its speed advantage at moderate accuracy near
$n\!\approx\!34$--$48$ --- always in terms of the \emph{compiled peak rank},
which for most circuits is far below the qubit count.
\item \textbf{Norm estimation} is the accuracy-cost bottleneck for generic
non-product circuits that do not end fully collapsed
($\chi L\sim1/\delta^4$); the clean results lean on the analytic and rank-1
normalization regimes.
\item \textbf{Episodic compression of full-record probabilities} degrades
sharply below the per-episode exact budget (\S\ref{sec:episodic});
episodic-exact carries no such caveat.
\item \textbf{The frame's advantage is constant/poly, not an exponent}, with
substantial static prior
art~\cite{bravyi2016,qassim2019,garcia2015,pashayan2022}; its measured value
is confined to Clifford-dominated adaptive circuits
(Table~\ref{tab:natural}).
\item \textbf{Scale-arm gaps:} the C\texttt{++} pipeline is build-and-query
only (no measurement path --- the gadgetized route removes the need for one
in strong simulation) and consumes plain gate streams rather than HIR; the
Python engine's sampling measurement path and canonical dedup materialize
$2^n$ (validation-scale only; the forced-replay and episodic paths are
non-materializing). The adaptive wall-clock numbers are Python-vs-Python
(fair internally, absolute constants not comparable to C\texttt{++} tools).
\item \texttt{quEStab} (ACM ICS 2026, multi-GPU extended stabilizer) still
needs a manual literature check (paywalled, no preprint).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
The system is one compiler with two executors. \texttt{clifft}'s compiler
reduces every circuit to a Clifford-free Heisenberg IR and, in doing so,
computes the very quantities ($k$, $t_{\rm live}$, $m_{\rm blk}$, $R$) that
price four execution strategies before anything runs. The dense engine keeps
its exactness contract and its dominance wherever the compiled block is
small --- which, by the compiler's own strength, is most circuits. The
CH-form backend extends reach where the block is large but magic is sparse:
measured crossovers at $n\!\approx\!34$--$48$ against the true exact fast
path, sole feasibility past $n\!\approx\!62$, a predictable accuracy dial
($\mathrm{TV}=0.50\,\delta$), generality over arbitrary Clifford$+T$
circuits via gadgetization, adaptive circuits via the online frame (winning
precisely on the fault-tolerance-shaped workloads it targets), and
episode-structured computations at the per-episode exponent. Each claim
carries its measured boundary: where \texttt{clifft} wins, where the
estimator degrades, and where the only honest answer is ``infeasible''.
